classification.difficultyReason: Requires a domain-restricted semicircle comparison with a line and rejection of the extraneous intersection introduced by squaring.

inlines.text: Use the part of the upper semicircle on or above the line, within

answer.worked:
Sketch the upper semicircle $y=\sqrt{16-x^2}$, whose domain is $-4\le x\le4$, and the line $y=x+2$.

An intersection must have $x+2\ge0$. Squaring the equality gives
$$\begin{align*}16-x^2&=(x+2)^2\\16-x^2&=x^2+4x+4\\x^2+2x-6&=0\\x&=-1\pm\sqrt7.\end{align*}$$
The value $-1-\sqrt7$ makes $x+2<0$, so it is not an intersection of the original graphs. The intersection has $x=-1+\sqrt7$.

The upper semicircle is on or above the line from its left endpoint to this intersection. Therefore
$$-4\le x\le-1+\sqrt7.$$
